practice.passage_title: Should the School Reduce Plastic?
practice.passage: The student council proposed replacing some single-use lunch packaging with reusable containers. Its argument began with a clear claim: the school should run a four-week trial before making a permanent purchase. The council’s fictional classroom survey found that 72 of 120 respondents supported the trial. A second source, a cafeteria cost table, estimated that washing reusable containers would require additional time. Supporters argued that the trial could measure both waste and labor instead of assuming that one benefit settled the whole question. Critics worried about lost containers and unequal access to supplies. The proposal responded by lending containers during the trial and counting losses. The council did not claim that a survey proved the policy would work. It used the survey to show interest and proposed collecting direct evidence of costs and waste.

practice.title: ELA
practice.passage_title: Arachne: an Original Retelling
practice.passage: This original retelling draws on the traditional myth. Arachne was a talented weaver who took great pride in her work. When people praised her skill, she insisted that no teacher or goddess deserved any credit. Athena, associated with wisdom and crafts, approached in disguise and advised her to speak with humility. Arachne dismissed the advice and demanded a contest. The two wove remarkable pictures, but their conflict involved more than technical skill: Arachne’s attitude challenged the goddess’s authority. In the traditional ending, Athena transformed Arachne into a spider, forever connected with weaving. Readers can admire Arachne’s ability while questioning her boastfulness and the severity of the punishment. The story invites discussion of pride, power, artistic skill, and the consequences of refusing advice. A theme is a reasoned interpretation, not simply the name of a topic.

practice.passage_title: The Bridge Apprentice
practice.passage: In this original historical fiction, an apprentice watched an experienced builder inspect a Roman-style stone bridge. The apprentice wanted to remove the wooden supports as soon as the final stone was placed. "A finished appearance is not enough," the builder warned. He checked the arch and explained how its stones pressed against one another and transferred forces toward the supports. The apprentice grew impatient, but a cracked stone changed her mind. Together they replaced it and repeated the inspection. Later, the apprentice wrote that the delay had been the most important part of the work. The scene does not establish facts about a particular ancient builder; it uses an imagined conversation to explore patience and responsibility. Readers should distinguish the fictional characters from historical claims, such as the Romans’ use of arches in engineering.

practice.passage_title: An Argument for Trees
practice.passage: A community group argues that a school should plant trees near its outdoor learning area. Its claim is narrower than "trees solve every problem": a carefully chosen location may provide shade and support habitat. The group presents a fictional class data table comparing temperatures at a sunny spot and a shaded spot. It also acknowledges counterarguments: planting and watering cost money, and roots or branches may interfere with structures. Its proposal recommends consulting knowledgeable staff, selecting a suitable location, and comparing costs before planting. An effective response to a counterargument does not mock the people who raise it. Instead, it explains how the plan addresses a reasonable concern or why the evidence supports a different choice. The final paragraph asks the school to try a manageable plan and report the results.

practice.passage: Our reading area should have a shaded bench. At noon, the sunny bench can be uncomfortable. A shaded seat would give readers another choice. The street unrolls its silver thread,
The restless clouds move overhead.
A window holds the fading light;
A branch writes slowly into night.

And hear the roof repeat its eaves.
The storm has gone; its quiet trace
Still draws a map across this place.

practice.title: ELA
practice.passage_title: The Printer’s Workshop
practice.passage:
Original drama:
[An apprentice arranges metal type on a table.]
APPRENTICE: If we print the same page many times, will every reader agree with it?
PRINTER: Copies spread words, not agreement.
APPRENTICE: Then accuracy matters before the first copy.
[The printer points to a misplaced letter.]
PRINTER: And readers must question what they read.

Informational companion: In early modern Europe, printing made it possible to reproduce texts more quickly than copying each one by hand. Printed works helped ideas circulate, including religious, scientific, and artistic arguments. Access remained uneven; not everyone could read or obtain books. Greater circulation did not guarantee that every claim was true. Scholars therefore needed observation, reasoning, and the comparison of sources as well as access to texts.

practice.title: ELA
practice.passage_title: A History Portfolio
practice.passage: A student created a portfolio about how travel and communication changed societies. She began with a research question rather than a list of famous people: How did networks connect communities, and whose experiences were left out of the usual accounts? She compared a map, a trade-route reading, and a translated historical account. Her notes separated quotations, paraphrases, and her own interpretations. When two accounts disagreed, she recorded their authors, purposes, and contexts instead of choosing the more dramatic version. The final presentation used a timeline but did not imply that every change happened everywhere at once. It included an argument supported by evidence and a section explaining limitations. The student concluded that a strong portfolio shows not only a polished product but also how the researcher checked and revised the work.

items.prompt: Write a focused research question connected to the passage.
What does the student do when accounts disagree?
How do matter cycles differ from energy flow through an ecosystem?

When two accounts disagreed, she recorded their authors, purposes, and contexts instead of choosing the more dramatic version. The final presentation used a timeline but did not imply that every change happened everywhere at once. It included an argument supported by evidence and a section explaining limitations. The student concluded that a strong portfolio shows not only a polished product but also how the researcher checked and revised the work.
